question: My lease in Florida is over and I have moved out. My landlord says he is not claiming any damage. How long does he have to give my security deposit back?
reference_answer: If the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, it must return the deposit, together with any interest that is owed, within 15 days after the rental agreement ends (Fla. Stat. s. 83.49(3)(a)).

question: My former landlord in Florida says he will keep part of my deposit for damage, and he sent me the notice by e-mail. Is e-mail allowed, and what deadlines apply?
reference_answer: A landlord who intends to claim part of the deposit must, within 30 days after the rental agreement ends, give the tenant written notice of its intention to impose the claim and the reason for it, by certified mail to the tenant's last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 (Fla. Stat. s. 83.49(3)(a)). E-mail delivery is valid only if the landlord and tenant signed an addendum to the rental agreement agreeing to electronic delivery of notices, each giving a valid e-mail address (s. 83.505(1)); without that addendum an e-mailed claim notice does not meet the statute. A landlord that misses the 30 days forfeits the right to impose the claim on the deposit, although it may still sue for damages after returning the deposit (s. 83.49(3)(a)). The tenant then has 15 days after receiving a proper notice to object; unless the tenant objects in time, the landlord may deduct the claim and must remit the balance within 30 days after the date of the notice (s. 83.49(3)(b)).

question: I rent my Florida apartment month to month with no written lease. How much notice does either of us have to give to end the tenancy?
reference_answer: A tenancy from month to month may be ended by either party giving written notice of not less than 30 days before the end of any monthly period (Fla. Stat. s. 83.57(3)). The notice must be delivered in the manner s. 83.56(4) provides.

question: I am a few days late with my rent in Florida. What does my landlord have to do before he can end my lease for not paying?
reference_answer: The landlord must deliver a written demand for payment of the rent or possession of the premises. If the default continues for 3 days after delivery, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and court-observed legal holidays, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. The notice must contain a statement in substantially the form the statute sets out (Fla. Stat. s. 83.56(3)), and the rental agreement cannot waive these notice requirements (s. 83.56(4)).

question: My Florida landlord threatened to change the locks and turn off the water if I do not pay today. Can he do that?
reference_answer: No. A landlord may not cause, directly or indirectly, the termination or interruption of any utility service furnished to the tenant, such as water, electricity or gas, whether or not the landlord controls or pays for it (Fla. Stat. s. 83.67(1)), and may not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit, for example by changing the locks (s. 83.67(2)). A landlord who does so is liable to the tenant for actual and consequential damages or 3 months' rent, whichever is greater, and for costs including attorney's fees (s. 83.67(6)).

question: The condo association in my Florida building requires new tenants to place a security deposit with it. My rent is $2,400 a month. What is the most the association may ask for?
reference_answer: $2,400. question: The owner of the Florida condo I rent has stopped paying the association, and the association wrote to me demanding that I pay my rent to it. Do I have to, and does that protect me from my landlord?
reference_answer: Yes. If the unit owner is delinquent in paying a monetary obligation to the association, the association may make a written demand that the tenant pay the subsequent rent to the association until all of the owner's obligations are paid in full, and the tenant must pay the association until it releases the tenant or the tenancy ends. The association must give the tenant a notice in the form the statute sets out and mail written notice of its demand to the unit owner. A tenant is immune from any claim by the landlord or unit owner related to the rent timely paid to the association after the demand (Fla. Stat. s. 718.116(11)).

question: In the lease fl-lease-01, clause 9 says the tenant waives all rights, remedies and notices given to tenants by part II of chapter 83, including the three-day notice before the landlord ends the lease for unpaid rent. Is that enforceable in Florida?
reference_answer: No. A provision in a rental agreement is void and unenforceable to the extent that it purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies or requirements set forth in part II of chapter 83 (Fla. Stat. s. 83.47(1)(a)). The lease's waiver of every right and notice under part II is therefore void to that extent, and if either party suffers actual damages as a result of such a provision being included, the aggrieved party may recover them (s. 83.47(2)).

question: In the lease fl-lease-02, a Fort Lauderdale condominium, clauses 10 to 12 make a married couple pay the association $150 each to approve the lease, pay it again at each renewal, and place a deposit of $5,600, two months' rent, with the association. Are those charges allowed?
reference_answer: Not as written. Stat. s. 718.112(2)(k)).

question: I rent an apartment in a Florida building with many units. What does my landlord have to provide about pests, locks, common areas, garbage, heat and water?
reference_answer: At all times during the tenancy the landlord must comply with the applicable building, housing and health codes or, where there are none, keep the structure in good repair and the plumbing in reasonable working condition (Fla. Stat. s. 83.51(1)). For a unit that is not a single-family home or a duplex, and unless otherwise agreed in writing, the landlord must also make reasonable provisions for the extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms and bedbugs; locks and keys; the clean and safe condition of common areas; garbage removal and outside receptacles; and functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water and hot water (s. 83.51(2)(a)).

question: I am renting a single-family house in Florida. Does my landlord have to put in smoke detectors?
reference_answer: Yes, unless the landlord and tenant agree otherwise in writing. At the commencement of the tenancy of a single-family home or duplex, the landlord shall install working smoke detection devices, meaning electrical or battery-operated devices that detect particles of combustion and are listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory (Fla. Stat. s. 83.51(2)(b)).

question: What am I responsible for as a tenant in Florida, apart from paying rent?
reference_answer: At all times during the tenancy the tenant must comply with the obligations the building, housing and health codes put on tenants; keep the part of the premises he occupies and uses clean and sanitary; remove garbage from the unit in a clean and sanitary way; keep the plumbing fixtures he uses clean, sanitary and in repair; use and operate reasonably the electrical, plumbing, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances; not destroy, deface, damage, impair or remove any part of the premises or the landlord's property, nor allow anyone else to; and conduct himself, and require others on the premises with his consent to conduct themselves, so as not to disturb the neighbors unreasonably or breach the peace (Fla. question: Can my Florida landlord walk into my apartment without telling me first?
reference_answer: Not freely. The landlord may enter at any time for the protection or preservation of the premises, as in an emergency. To make repairs he may enter on reasonable notice and at a reasonable time: at least 24 hours' notice, between 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. For the other purposes the statute lists (to inspect, supply agreed services, or show the unit to buyers, workers and others) he may enter with the tenant's consent, in an emergency, when the tenant unreasonably withholds consent, or when the tenant is absent for half the time between rent payments (but if the rent is current and the tenant has said he will be away, only with consent or for the protection or preservation of the premises). The tenant must not unreasonably withhold consent, and the landlord must not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant (Fla. Stat. s. 83.53).

question: When does a Florida landlord have to give a tenant a flood disclosure, and what can the tenant do if he does not?
reference_answer: A landlord must complete and give the prospective tenant a flood disclosure, in a separate document and in substantially the form the statute sets out, at or before the signing of a rental agreement for a term of one year or longer (Fla. Stat. s. 83.512(1)). If the landlord violates this and the tenant suffers a substantial loss or damage to personal property from flooding, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement by written notice and by surrendering possession no later than 30 days after the date of the damage or loss; 'substantial' means that repairing or replacing the property costs 50 percent or more of its market value on the date of the flood (s. 83.512(2)). The landlord must refund rent and other amounts paid in advance for any period after the termination takes effect (s. 83.512(3)).

question: I pay my Florida rent monthly and my lease does not say how long the tenancy lasts. How long is it, and when is the rent due?
reference_answer: If the rental agreement says nothing about the duration, it is set by the period for which the rent is payable, so a tenancy with monthly rent is from month to month (Fla. Stat. s. 83.46(2)). Unless otherwise agreed, rent is payable without demand or notice, periodic rent is payable at the beginning of each rent payment period, and rent is apportionable from day to day (s. 83.46(1)).

question: Does my Florida landlord have to tell me who I can send notices to?
reference_answer: Yes. The landlord, or a person authorized to enter into a rental agreement for him, must disclose in writing to the tenant, at or before the start of the tenancy, the name and address of the landlord or of a person authorized to receive notices and demands on his behalf. That person keeps the authority until the tenant is notified otherwise, and notices of such names and addresses, or changes to them, are delivered to the tenant's residence or to another address the tenant specifies in writing, or may be sent by e-mail under s. 83.505 (Fla. Stat. s. 83.50).

question: I complained to the county's code enforcement about mold in my Florida apartment, and now my landlord says he will evict me. Is that allowed?
reference_answer: It may be unlawful. A landlord may not discriminatorily increase the rent, decrease services, or bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or another civil action, primarily because he is retaliating against the tenant; complaining to a governmental agency responsible for enforcing a building, housing or health code about a suspected violation is one of the listed examples. The tenant must have acted in good faith, and may raise retaliation as a defense in an action for possession (Fla. Stat. s. 83.64(1) and (2)). It does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause, such as a good-faith action for nonpayment of rent or a violation of the rental agreement or the statute (s. 83.64(3)).

question: My Florida landlord ignores my written complaints about a leaking roof. Can I just stop paying rent, and what happens if he sues me for it?
reference_answer: Not safely without following the statute. A landlord must keep roofs and other structural components in good repair, or comply with the applicable building, housing and health codes (Fla. Stat. s. 83.51(1)). If he materially fails to, the tenant may give written notice specifying the noncompliance and his intention to stop paying rent because of it; once 7 days have passed after delivery, the noncompliance can be raised as a defense (s. 83.60(1)(b)). In that case, a material noncompliance is a complete defense to an action for possession based on nonpayment, and the court determines the amount by which the rent is reduced for the lost value of the unit. A tenant who raises any defense other than payment in an action for possession must pay the accrued rent, and the rent that falls due during the case, into the court registry, or file a motion to determine the rent, within 5 days after service (excluding weekends and legal holidays), or he waives the defenses and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment (s. 83.60(2)). The tenant may instead terminate the agreement if the landlord fails to comply within 7 days after written notice (s. 83.56(1)).

question: I am a servicemember with orders to move 200 miles away. Can I end my Florida lease early, and what must I give my landlord?
reference_answer: Yes. A servicemember may end his rental agreement by giving the landlord written notice, effective on the date stated in it, which must be at least 30 days after the landlord receives it, if he is required by permanent change of station orders to move 35 miles or more from the rental premises (Fla. Stat. s. 83.682(1)(a)). The notice must come with a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by his commanding officer (s. 83.682(2)). A landlord may not retaliate against a servicemember who has terminated a rental agreement under that section (s. 83.64(1)(d)).

question: A fire made my Florida apartment unusable through no fault of mine. Can I leave, and what happens to my deposit and belongings?
reference_answer: If the premises are damaged or destroyed other than by the tenant's wrongful or negligent acts so that the enjoyment of the premises is substantially impaired, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement and vacate immediately, or may vacate only the part rendered unusable, in which case the rent is reduced by the fair rental value of that part (Fla. Stat. s. 83.63(1)). If the agreement is terminated, the landlord must handle the deposit as s. 83.49(3) requires: return it within 15 days, or give written notice of a claim within 30 days. The tenant must also be given the opportunity to collect his belongings when it is safe, or notice of a date within a reasonable time by which he can (s. 83.63(2)).

question: If I take my Florida landlord to court over my security deposit and win, who pays the attorney fees, and can my lease say otherwise?
reference_answer: The loser pays. In an action to adjudicate the right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable attorney's fee, and the court must advance the cause on the calendar (Fla. Stat. s. 83.49(3)(c)). More generally, in any civil action to enforce the rental agreement or part II of chapter 83, the party in whose favor judgment is rendered may recover reasonable attorney fees and court costs from the nonprevailing party, and this right may not be waived in a lease; the exception is a claim for personal injury damages based on a breach of the landlord's maintenance duty under s. 83.51 (s. 83.48).

question: My Florida rent is $1,500 a month. An addendum I signed says that if I end my lease early I pay a $4,000 early termination fee and give 90 days' notice. Does the statute allow that?
reference_answer: No. A landlord may charge liquidated damages or an early termination fee only if the amount does not exceed 2 months' rent, here $3,000, and, for an early termination fee, only if the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days' notice before the proposed termination date. The remedy is available only if the tenant accepted it at signing by signing a separate addendum in substantially the form the statute sets out (Fla. Stat. s. 83.595(4)). A fee of $4,000 with 90 days' notice exceeds both limits.

question: I rent my main home in Spain from a private owner and signed a one-year contract. When the year ends, can the landlord make me leave, or can I stay on?
reference_answer: The parties may agree any duration, but if it is shorter than five years (seven if the landlord is a legal person), then when the term ends the contract is extended obligatorily by yearly periods until it reaches five years (seven), unless the tenant tells the landlord at least 30 days before the end of the term, or of any extension, that he does not want to renew (art. 9.1 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). So the tenant may stay on, and the landlord cannot end the contract at the end of the first year. The exception is a landlord who is a natural person and whose contract stated expressly, when it was signed, that he needs the home before five years have passed for himself or for a first-degree relative: after the first year he may then recover it by giving at least two months' notice (art. 9.3).

question: How many months of deposit can a landlord in Spain ask for when I sign a lease for my home, and can he also ask me for a bank guarantee?
reference_answer: When the contract is signed the landlord must require a cash deposit (fianza) equal to one month's rent for a dwelling (art. 36.1 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). The parties may also agree any other guarantee, such as a bank guarantee, in addition to the cash deposit, but for a housing lease of up to five years (up to seven if the landlord is a legal person) the value of that additional guarantee may not exceed two months' rent (art. 36.5).
source_note: Ministerio de Vivienda y Agenda Urbana, 'Alquila bien, es tu derecho: Preguntas frecuentes' (https://www.mivau.gob.es/vivienda/alquila-bien-es-tu-derecho/alquiler/10-preguntas), read on 2026-10-20: questions 7 and 9 (how many months of deposit may be required, and whether a bank guarantee may). The question is my own phrasing of that topic.

question: Can I sublet one room of the flat I rent in Spain without asking my landlord?
reference_answer: No. A rented dwelling may be sublet only in part, and only with the landlord's prior written consent (art. 8.2 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos); the tenant also cannot assign the contract without the landlord's written consent (art. 8.1). A subtenant's right ends whenever the tenant's own right does.

question: My tenant in Spain has stopped paying the rent. Can I end the contract because of that?
reference_answer: Yes. If a party fails to meet its obligations under the contract, the party that has met its own may demand performance or seek termination of the contract under art. 1124 of the Civil Code (art. 27.1 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). In addition, the landlord may terminate the contract by operation of law (de pleno derecho) for non-payment of the rent or of any other amount the tenant has taken on or must pay (art. 27.2.a). How possession is then recovered in court is procedural law, which Plumbline has not indexed.

question: A landlord in Spain wants me to pay a month's deposit now, before I have even seen the flat, and a second deposit later. How much can a landlord legitimately require from me up front under Spanish law?
reference_answer: The Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos sets three limits for a housing lease. The landlord may never require payment in advance of more than one month's rent (art. 17.2). At signing the landlord must require a cash deposit (fianza) of one month's rent (art. 36.1). Any other guarantee the parties agree in addition may not exceed two months' rent in a lease of up to five years, or seven if the landlord is a legal person (art. 36.5). So one month's deposit plus a second month as an additional guarantee fits within the statute, and the guarantee could go up to two months, but the landlord may not require more than that, and never more than one month's rent in advance. The indexed law does not regulate payments to reserve a flat before a contract is signed.

question: Can the owners' community in my building in Spain stop a flat from being used as a tourist rental, and with what majority?
reference_answer: Yes. An express community agreement that approves, limits, conditions or prohibits the activity described in art. 5(e) of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos (the temporary letting of a furnished, ready-to-use dwelling, marketed through tourist channels for profit and subject to a specific tourism regime), in the terms of the tourism legislation, needs the favourable vote of three fifths of all owners who also represent three fifths of the participation quotas, whether or not it changes the constitutive title or the statutes (art. 17.12 of the Ley de Propiedad Horizontal). The same majority can set special expense shares, or a larger share of the common expenses, for the flat where the activity takes place, as long as the increase is no more than 20%. These agreements have no retroactive effect.
source_note: Ministerio de Vivienda y Agenda Urbana, 'Alquila bien, es tu derecho: Preguntas frecuentes' (https://www.mivau.gob.es/vivienda/alquila-bien-es-tu-derecho/alquiler/10-preguntas), read on 2026-10-20: question 10 (what residents' communities can do about tourist rentals). question: My landlord in Spain wants to do works in the flat I rent. When do I have to put up with them, can I leave, and what if the flat becomes uninhabitable?
reference_answer: Improvement works (art. 22 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos): the tenant must put up with works that cannot reasonably be postponed until the lease ends. The landlord must notify the tenant in writing at least three months ahead of their nature, start, duration and foreseeable cost. During the month after that notice the tenant may withdraw from the contract, unless the works do not affect the dwelling or affect it only trivially; the lease then ends within two months of the withdrawal, and the works may not start during them. The tenant is entitled to a rent reduction in proportion to the part of the dwelling he is deprived of, and to compensation for expenses the works force on him (art. 22.3). Conservation works that cannot reasonably be postponed must be tolerated even if very inconvenient or if they deprive the tenant of part of the home; if they last more than twenty days, the rent must be reduced in proportion to the part he is deprived of (art. 21.2). If conservation works, or works ordered by a competent authority, make the dwelling uninhabitable, the tenant may suspend the contract or withdraw from it without any compensation; suspension stops the contract's term and the obligation to pay rent until the works end (art. 26).

question: A private individual and I signed a lease for his flat in Spain on 10 February 2019. What minimum duration did the law in force that day give me?
reference_answer: Three years. On 10 February 2019 art. 9.1 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos read as restored on 24 January 2019, when Congress repealed Real Decreto-ley 21/2018: a lease shorter than three years was extended obligatorily by yearly periods until it reached a minimum duration of three years, unless the tenant gave 30 days' notice of not renewing. The five-year minimum (seven if the landlord is a legal person) applies only from 6 March 2019, when Real Decreto-ley 7/2019 took effect.

question: I signed a rental contract in Spain on 1 March 2022 with a landlord who is a private individual, not a company, and his agent charged me the agency's fee. On that date, did the law make those costs the landlord's?
reference_answer: Not for a landlord who is a natural person. On 1 March 2022 the last sentence of art. 20.1 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos said that property-management and contract-formalisation costs were the landlord's when the landlord is a legal person; it set no such rule for a private individual, so the statute did not by itself bar the agent's fee being charged to the tenant. Since Ley 12/2023 took effect on 26 May 2023 these costs are the landlord's whoever he is.

question: I rent my home in Spain and want to leave after eight months. As the law stood in March 2026, what notice did I have to give, and could my landlord claim compensation?
reference_answer: Once at least six months have passed, the tenant may withdraw from the contract by notifying the landlord at least 30 days in advance (art. 11 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos, as in force on 1 March 2026). The parties may have agreed in the contract that the tenant must then compensate the landlord with an amount equal to one month of the rent in force for each year of the contract still to run, with periods shorter than a year giving a proportional part. The statute itself provides for compensation only through such an agreement.

question: In the lease es-lease-03, a Seville flat let by a private individual, clause 5 lets the landlord end the lease at any time on fifteen days' notice if he needs the flat for himself or his family. Is that valid under Spanish law on the signing date?
reference_answer: No. A landlord who is a natural person may recover the dwelling for himself or a first-degree relative only after the first year of the contract, only if the contract stated expressly when it was signed that he needs it before five years have passed, and by giving at least two months' notice (art. 9.3 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). A right to end the lease at any time on fifteen days' notice does not meet those conditions.

question: Can I knock down a wall or otherwise change the layout of the flat I rent in Spain without my landlord's agreement?
reference_answer: No. The tenant may not carry out, without the landlord's written consent, works that change the configuration of the dwelling or of its accessories, and in no case works that reduce the dwelling's stability or safety (art. 23.1 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). If the landlord did not authorise them, then, without prejudice to his power to terminate the contract, he may require at the end of the lease that the tenant restore things to their former state, or keep the change without compensating the tenant; and if the works reduced the building's stability or the dwelling's safety, he may require immediate restoration (art. 23.2).

question: I have a disability and need to adapt the inside of the flat I rent in Spain. Can I do the works without my landlord's consent?
reference_answer: Yes, after notifying the landlord in writing. The tenant may carry out inside the dwelling the works or measures needed for it to be used in a way suited to a disability, or to an age over seventy, of the tenant himself, his spouse, the person who lives with him in an analogous relationship, or relatives who live permanently with either of them, provided the works do not affect common elements or services of the building and do not reduce its stability or safety (art. 24.1 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). At the end of the contract the tenant must restore the dwelling to its former state if the landlord requires it (art. 24.2).

question: My landlord in Spain has paid for improvement works. Can he raise my rent because of them?
reference_answer: After five years of the contract (seven if the landlord is a legal person), and unless otherwise agreed, yes: improvement works entitle the landlord to raise the annual rent by the amount that results from applying to the capital invested, less any public subsidies, the legal interest rate of money when the works end plus three points, without the increase exceeding 20% of the rent in force then (art. 19.1 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). The increase applies from the month after the landlord notifies the tenant in writing of its amount, detailing the calculation and attaching copies of the documents showing the cost (art. 19.3). Separately, at any time the parties may agree improvement works and a rent increase (art. 19.4).

question: The tenant of our flat in Spain wants to leave without telling his wife, who lives with him. Can the lease continue for her?
reference_answer: Yes. If the tenant says he will not renew the contract, or withdraws from it, without the consent of the spouse who lived with him, the lease may continue for that spouse (art. 12.1 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). The landlord may require the spouse to state her wishes; if she does not answer within fifteen days of the request, the lease ends, and she must pay the rent up to its end if it has not been paid (art. 12.2). If the tenant leaves without expressly withdrawing, the lease may continue for the spouse if, within a month of the abandonment, the landlord receives her written notice that she wants to be the tenant; if the lease ends for lack of notice, she owes that month's rent (art. 12.3). The same applies to a person who has lived with the tenant permanently in an analogous relationship for at least the two years before the withdrawal or abandonment, or any length of time if they had children together (art. 12.4).

question: My husband is the tenant of our flat in Spain and we are divorcing. Can I stay in the flat as the tenant?
reference_answer: If the flat is attributed to you under the applicable civil law, yes. In cases of nullity of the marriage, judicial separation or divorce of the tenant, the spouse who is not the tenant may continue to use the rented dwelling when it is attributed to her under the applicable civil law, and the spouse to whom its use is attributed permanently, or for longer than the time left of the lease, becomes the holder of the contract (art. 15.1 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). She must tell the landlord of her wish to continue within two months of being notified of the court's decision, enclosing a copy of it or of the part that affects the use of the dwelling (art. 15.2).

question: My lease in Spain says I give up my rights under the tenancy law. Is that clause valid?
reference_answer: Not if it works against you. Stipulations that modify, to the detriment of the tenant or the subtenant, the rules of the title on housing leases are void and are treated as unwritten, except where the rule itself expressly allows them (art. 6 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos).

question: The bank has foreclosed on my landlord's building in Spain and the flat I rent was sold. Do I have to leave?
reference_answer: Not necessarily. If during the first five years of the contract (seven if the landlord is a legal person) the landlord's right is extinguished by, among other causes, a forced sale arising from a mortgage foreclosure or a court judgment, the tenant has the right in any case to continue in the lease until five (or seven) years are completed, without prejudice to the tenant's power not to renew under art. 9.1 (art. 13.1 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). In a lease agreed for longer than five (seven) years, if the landlord's right is extinguished by one of those causes after the first five (seven) years, the lease ends, unless it was registered in the Property Registry before the rights that caused the extinction, in which case it continues for the agreed duration.

question: Does my landlord in Spain have to give me a receipt when I pay the rent?
reference_answer: Yes, unless the parties agreed that payment is made by a procedure that itself proves that the tenant has paid, such as a bank transfer. The receipt, or the document that replaces it, must show separately the amounts paid for the different items that make up the total payment and, specifically, the rent in force. If the landlord does not give the receipt, all the costs the tenant incurs to record the payment are the landlord's (art. 17.4 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos).

question: A pipe burst in my rented flat in Spain and I cannot reach my landlord. Can I have it repaired and charge him?
reference_answer: Yes, for urgent repairs, if you first inform him. The tenant must tell the landlord as soon as possible of the need for the repairs the landlord owes, letting him check the dwelling directly, and at any time, after informing the landlord, he may carry out the repairs that are urgent to avoid imminent damage or serious inconvenience and demand their cost from the landlord at once (art. 21.3 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). Small repairs that ordinary wear and tear requires are the tenant's own (art. 21.4).

question: My husband is the tenant of our flat in Spain. If he moves out, or if we divorce, can I stay on in the flat?
reference_answer: In both cases the law protects the spouse who is not the tenant, with deadlines. If he withdraws from the contract or says he will not renew it without your consent, the lease may continue for you; the landlord may require you to state your wishes, and the lease ends if you do not answer within fifteen days. If he simply leaves, the lease may continue for you if, within a month, the landlord receives your written notice that you want to be the tenant (art. 12 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). If the marriage is annulled, or you separate judicially or divorce, you may continue to use the dwelling when it is attributed to you under the applicable civil law, and you become the holder of the contract if the attribution is permanent or lasts longer than the rest of the lease; you must tell the landlord within two months of being notified of the court's decision, with a copy of it (art. 15).

question: My landlord in Spain might lose the building to a mortgage foreclosure, or sell it voluntarily. In which case do I keep my lease, and for how long?
reference_answer: In both you are protected for the first five years of the contract (seven if the landlord is a legal person). If the building is sold voluntarily, the buyer is subrogated in the landlord's rights and obligations for that period even if he meets the requirements of art. 34 of the Mortgage Law; if the agreed duration is longer, he is subrogated for all of it unless he meets those requirements, in which case he must bear the lease only for the time left of the five (seven) years and the seller must compensate you with one month's rent for each remaining year beyond it (art. 14 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). If the landlord's right is extinguished by a forced sale from a mortgage foreclosure, you may in any case continue until five (seven) years are completed; for a longer lease the lease ends after that period unless it was registered in the Property Registry before the rights that caused the extinction (art. 13.1).

question: Which changes can a tenant make to a rented flat in Spain, and which need the landlord's consent?
reference_answer: Works that change the dwelling's configuration or its accessories need the landlord's written consent, and works that reduce its stability or safety are never allowed; without consent the landlord may, at the end of the lease, require restoration or keep the change without compensation, and may require immediate restoration if stability or safety suffered (art. 23 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). The exception is works inside the dwelling needed to adapt it to a disability, or to an age over seventy, of the tenant, his partner or relatives living with him: they need only prior written notice to the landlord, provided they do not affect common elements or reduce stability or safety, and the tenant must restore the dwelling if the landlord requires it at the end of the contract (art. 24).

question: My landlord in Spain is a private individual and our contract is six years old. He spent EUR 12,000 on improvements and received a EUR 2,000 subsidy; the legal interest rate was 3.25% when the works ended, and my rent is EUR 900 a month. By how much a year may he raise it?
reference_answer: By EUR 625 a year. The capital invested is the cost less the subsidy: 12,000 - 2,000 = 10,000. The rate is the legal interest rate when the works ended plus three points: 3.25% + 3 = 6.25%, and 10,000 x 6.25% = 625 a year. question: In Colombia, how much can a landlord charge per month for a rented apartment, in relation to the apartment's value?
reference_answer: The monthly rent is fixed by the parties in legal currency, but it may not exceed one percent (1%) of the commercial value of the property, or of the part of it that is rented out. question: My landlord in Colombia wants to raise my rent. How often can he do it, by how much, and what does he have to do?
reference_answer: After each twelve months of the contract running at the same price, the landlord may raise the rent by up to 100% of the increase in the consumer price index in the calendar year before the one in which the increase is made, provided the new rent does not exceed the limit set by art. 18. A landlord who chooses to increase it must tell the tenant the amount and the date it takes effect, through the authorised postal service or the personal-notification mechanism the contract expressly provides, otherwise the increase cannot be enforced against the tenant. If the tenant pays an increase anyway, the lack of notice does not entitle him to a refund (art. 20 of Ley 820 de 2003).

question: I want to leave the apartment I rent in Colombia. What notice do I have to give, and do I owe the landlord anything?
reference_answer: It depends on when you leave. During the initial term or an extension, the tenant may end the contract unilaterally by giving the landlord at least three months' prior written notice through the authorised postal service and paying compensation equal to three months' rent; once those conditions are met the landlord must take back the property (art. 24, point 4, of Ley 820 de 2003). At the expiry of the initial term or of an extension, the tenant may end the contract by giving the same written notice at least three months before the expiry, without having to invoke any cause and without owing compensation; without written proof of the notice the contract renews automatically for a term equal to the one first agreed (art. 24, point 5).

The question is my own phrasing.

question: My landlord in Colombia wants his apartment back for his own use when my contract ends. What notice must he give me and what must he provide?
reference_answer: At the expiry of the initial term or of an extension, the landlord may end the contract by invoking a special ground, which includes needing to occupy the property as his own home for at least one year, with prior written notice to the tenant through the authorised postal service at least three months before the expiry. For that ground, and for demolition or repairs and for delivery under a sale contract, he must attach to the notice proof of a guarantee in cash, from a bank or from an insurance company, in the tenant's favour, equal to six months of the current rent, to guarantee that the ground is carried out within six months after the property is returned. Without written proof of the notice the contract renews automatically for a term equal to the initial one (art. 22, point 8, of Ley 820 de 2003).

The question is my own phrasing.

question: Can I sublet my rented apartment in Colombia, or hand my contract over to someone else?
reference_answer: Not on your own. The tenant has no power to assign the lease or to sublet unless the landlord expressly authorises it. If the tenant does so anyway, the landlord may end the contract and demand the property, or sign a new contract with the actual occupants, in which case the earlier contract has no effect, and either step is communicated to the tenant in writing (art. 17 of Ley 820 de 2003).

question: Can a landlord in Colombia ask me for a cash deposit when I rent a home?
reference_answer: Not to secure your obligations under the lease. In a housing lease no cash deposits or other real guarantees (cauciones reales) may be demanded to guarantee what the tenant owes under the contract, and such guarantees may not be stipulated indirectly, through an intermediary, in a document separate from the contract, or replaced by others under different names (art. 16 of Ley 820 de 2003). The exception concerns utilities: when the tenant is to pay for public utilities, the landlord may require guarantees or deposits to secure payment of each utility company's bills, which may not exceed the fixed charge, the connection charge and the consumption charge for two consecutive billing periods, and which the landlord then passes to the utility company (art. 15, point 1).

question: In a Colombian apartment building, who pays the monthly common-area fees (administración) when the apartment is rented out, the owner or the tenant?
reference_answer: Between landlord and tenant, the contract decides: the tenant must pay on time the utilities and the common expenses (expensas comunes) where they apply, as the contract provides (art. 9, point 3, of Ley 820 de 2003). Towards the building, the owners of the private units must contribute to the necessary common expenses under the horizontal-property regulation, and for the ordinary common expenses the owner and the holder (tenedor) of the unit under any title, such as a tenant, are jointly liable (art. 29 of Ley 675 de 2001), so the building may claim them from either.

question: My apartment in Colombia is appraised at COP 250,000,000 commercially, but its cadastral appraisal is COP 100,000,000. What is the most a landlord may charge me per month?
reference_answer: COP 2,000,000. The monthly rent may not exceed 1% of the property's commercial value, and for this purpose the commercial value cannot exceed twice the current cadastral appraisal, that is COP 200,000,000, which is less than the COP 250,000,000 appraisal; 1% of COP 200,000,000 is COP 2,000,000 (art. 18 of Ley 820 de 2003).

question: In the lease co-lease-02, a Medellín apartment, clause 3 sets the rent at COP 2,600,000 a month, and clause 4 records a commercial value of COP 220,000,000 and a cadastral appraisal of COP 95,000,000. Is that rent within the legal limit?
reference_answer: No. The monthly rent may not exceed 1% of the property's commercial value, and the commercial value cannot be counted as more than twice the current cadastral appraisal: twice COP 95,000,000 is COP 190,000,000, which is less than the COP 220,000,000 recorded, so the cap is 1% of COP 190,000,000, that is COP 1,900,000. The rent of COP 2,600,000 exceeds it (art. 18 of Ley 820 de 2003).

question: My landlord in Colombia and I signed a written lease two weeks ago and he has not given me my copy. Does he have to, and what happens if he does not?
reference_answer: Yes. When the housing lease is in writing, the landlord must give the tenant, and the co-signer (codeudor) where there is one, a copy of it with the original signatures, within ten days of the date the contract was made (art. 8, point 3, of Ley 820 de 2003). If he does not, the competent authority, at a party's request, can fine him an amount equal to three months' rent (parágrafo of art. 8).

question: I pay my rent in cash every month and my landlord in Colombia never gives me a receipt. Does he have to?
reference_answer: Yes. The landlord, or whoever is authorised to receive the rent, must issue a written receipt that states the date, the amount and the period the payment covers. If he refuses, the tenant can ask the competent authority to intervene (art. 11 of Ley 820 de 2003).

question: My landlord in Colombia refuses to accept my rent this month. How can I pay so that I am not treated as being in arrears?
reference_answer: When the landlord refuses to receive the payment on the agreed terms and at the agreed place, the tenant pays by depositing the rent in the landlord's favour in an entity authorised by the national government, in the place where the property is, within five business days after the end of the agreed period (art. 10, point 1, of Ley 820 de 2003). The entity keeps the original of the deposit slip and gives two duplicates, one for each party (points 2 and 3). The tenant must notify the landlord of the deposit by authorised postal service, enclosing the duplicate, within five days after the deposit (point 4). Not following this procedure puts the tenant in arrears (point 5). Later payments can be made the same way or directly to the landlord, at the tenant's choice (point 7).

question: My tenant in Colombia has not paid the building's administration fee, which our contract makes his responsibility. Can I end the lease because of that?
reference_answer: Yes, it is a ground. question: The fixed term of my apartment lease in Colombia is about to end and nobody has said anything. What happens if I stay?
reference_answer: A housing lease is understood to be extended (prórroga) on the same conditions and for the same initial term, as long as each party has complied with its obligations and the tenant accepts the rent adjustments that the law authorises (art. 6 of Ley 820 de 2003).

question: Does a housing lease in Colombia have to be in writing, and what must the parties agree on at a minimum?
reference_answer: No: the contract may be oral or written. In either case the parties must agree at least on: the names and identification of the contracting parties; the identification of the property; the part of the property that is let, where that applies, and the areas and services shared with the other occupants; the price and how it is paid; the list of connected and additional services, things or uses; the term of the contract; and which party pays the public utilities of the property (art. 3 of Ley 820 de 2003).

question: I rent a room in a boarding house (pensión) in Bogotá for six months, with meals and laundry included. Can I leave early, and on how much notice?
reference_answer: A lease of part of a property that is not independent, that necessarily includes additional services, things or uses and is agreed for less than one year is a pensión contract. In that case either party may end the contract before its term expires by giving ten days' prior notice, without any compensation (art. 4, point d, of Ley 820 de 2003).

question: Can the rent for an apartment in Colombia be set in US dollars? How is it paid?
reference_answer: Yes. The monthly rent the parties stipulate may be fixed in any currency, including a foreign one, but it is paid in Colombian legal currency at the market representative exchange rate on the date the obligation was incurred, unless the parties have agreed a different reference date or rate (art. 19 of Ley 820 de 2003).

question: I own an apartment in a Colombian building and my payment of the common expenses is late. What interest can the building charge, and can it publish my name?
reference_answer: Late payment of common expenses (expensas) bears default interest equal to one and a half times the current bank interest rate (interés bancario corriente) certified by the Superintendencia Bancaria, as the statute names it, unless the general assembly, by the quorum the building's rules set, fixes a lower rate. While the default lasts it may be made public in the building, and the assembly's minutes will list the owners in arrears. The notice may only be posted where there is no constant flow of visitors, in a way that guarantees the co-owners know of it (art. 30 and its parágrafo of Ley 675 de 2001).
source_note: Synthetic: written to cover default interest on common expenses in a horizontal-property building (Ley 675), which the Bogotá FAQ page and booklet do not pose as a question.

question: Ley 820 de 2003 is said to give eviction cases a preferential procedure decided in a single instance (art. 39). Is that article still in force?
reference_answer: No. The Senate's compilation of Ley 820 de 2003 marks art. 39 (Trámite preferente y única instancia) as repealed by subparagraph c) of art. 626 of Ley 1564 de 2012 (the Código General del Proceso), with effect from 1 January 2014 and subject to the transition rule in point 6 of art. 627 of that law. The compilation marks arts. 35, 36, 38 and 40 the same way. The corpus does not include Ley 1564 de 2012, so it cannot say which rule applies instead.

question: A tenant in a Colombian apartment building keeps holding loud parties at night, against the building's rules. What can the landlord do under the tenancy law, and what can the building itself do to the tenant?
reference_answer: Under Ley 820 de 2003, the tenant's repeated conduct that affects the neighbours' peace, duly proven before the police authority, is a ground on which the landlord may ask to end the lease (art. 22, point 4), and so is the tenant's breach of the building's horizontal-property rules when the dwelling is under that regime (art. 22, point 6). Separately, under Ley 675 de 2001 the building can sanction a breach of non-monetary obligations by owners, tenants (tenedores) or third parties they answer for, after a written request that gives a time to comply: publication of the list of infractors, successive fines each of at most twice the monthly necessary common expenses payable by the infractor and together at most ten times them, and restriction of the use of non-essential common areas such as party rooms and sports areas; essential common goods and those of exclusive use can never be restricted (art. 59).
source_note: Secretaría Distrital del Hábitat de Bogotá, 'Cartilla didáctica: Contratos de arrendamiento de vivienda' (https://www.habitatbogota.gov.co/sites/default/files/Cartilla%20arrendamientos%20FINAL.pdf, October 2020), read on 2026-10-20: the landlord's question on a tenant with coexistence problems in a horizontal-property building, which seeded the Ley 820 part; the comparison with the building's own sanctions (Ley 675 art. 59) is mine. question: My lease in Colombia was extended automatically for a second year. Now my landlord wants me out in 30 days and says he will pay nothing. Is that allowed, and how must he proceed if he wants to end it during an extension?
reference_answer: Not on those terms. During an extension the landlord may end the contract unilaterally only by written notice to the tenant through the authorised postal service at least three months in advance and by paying compensation equal to three months' rent (art. 22, point 7, of Ley 820 de 2003). To do so he must: (a) notify the tenant through the authorised postal service, giving the termination date and saying that the legal compensation will be paid; (b) deposit the compensation in the tenant's favour, at the disposal of the competent authority, in an entity authorised by the national government, within the three months before the termination date, calculated on the rent in force on the date of the notice; (c) have the deposit slip record its cause and the tenant's name and exact address; and (d) if the tenant returns the property on the date set, the tenant receives the compensation as the authority authorises (art. 23). If the tenant does not return the property, the landlord may get the deposited sum back and start the eviction process (art. 23, parágrafo 1).

question: My landlord in Colombia wants to end our lease when its term expires, simply because he wants to; we have had it for five years. He says he will pay my compensation after I have moved out. What are the rules?
reference_answer: At the expiry of the initial term or of an extension, a landlord may end the contract on any of the special grounds in art. 22, point 8, by written notice to the tenant through the authorised postal service at least three months before the expiry date. One of those grounds, d), is his full will to end the contract; it is available only if the contract has run for at least four years, and it obliges him to compensate the tenant with an amount equal to one and a half months' rent, paid through the procedure of art. 23. Without written proof of the notice, the contract is understood to be renewed automatically for a term equal to the initial one. Whenever the landlord has to compensate the tenant, the tenant cannot be deprived of the property without having received the payment beforehand or without the landlord having duly secured it (right of retention, art. 26): so paying only after the tenant has left does not satisfy the statute.

question: I gave my landlord in Colombia the required notice and deposited the compensation to leave my rental early, but now he refuses to take the keys back. What can I do?
reference_answer: Once the tenant has met the conditions for ending the contract early (written notice through the authorised postal service at least three months in advance, and compensation equal to three months' rent) the landlord is bound to receive the property; if he does not, the tenant may deliver it provisionally through the competent authority, without prejudice to going to court (art. 24, point 4, of Ley 820 de 2003). On the tenant's written request, once the conditions are shown to be met, the authority sets a date and time for the handover and summons both parties by authorised mail; if the landlord does not come, the property is handed to a custodian (secuestre) chosen from the list of court auxiliaries until it is delivered to the landlord, at the landlord's cost, and minutes of the handover are signed (art. 24, parágrafo). The compensation was to be deposited in the landlord's favour at the disposal of the authority (art. 25, point b); if the landlord does not receive the property the tenant is entitled to have the deposited sum returned, without prejudice to the provisional delivery (art. 25, parágrafo 1).
source_note: Secretaría Distrital del Hábitat de Bogotá, 'Cartilla didáctica: Contratos de arrendamiento de vivienda' (https://www.habitatbogota.gov.co/sites/default/files/Cartilla%20arrendamientos%20FINAL.pdf, October 2020), read on 2026-10-20: the tenants' question on whether the Secretaría del Hábitat receives a rented property provisionally when the landlord refuses to take it back. question: My rent in Colombia is COP 1,500,000 a month and the contract has run twelve months at that price. The apartment's commercial value is COP 400,000,000 and its cadastral appraisal is COP 220,000,000. If consumer prices rose 5.2% in the last calendar year, what is the most my landlord can charge from now on, and what must he do to raise it?
reference_answer: At most COP 1,578,000 a month. After each twelve months of the contract at the same price the landlord may raise the rent by up to 100% of the increase in the consumer price index in the calendar year before the one in which the increase is made, here 5.2%: 1,500,000 x 1.052 = 1,578,000 (an increase of COP 78,000), as long as the new rent does not exceed the cap in art. 18. That cap is 1% of the commercial value, which cannot be counted as more than twice the cadastral appraisal (440,000,000): 1% of 400,000,000 is COP 4,000,000, so the cap does not limit this increase. He must tell the tenant the amount and the date it takes effect, through the authorised postal service or the personal-notification mechanism the contract expressly provides; otherwise the increase cannot be enforced against the tenant (art. 20 of Ley 820 de 2003).

question: My lease in Colombia started on 2021-06-16 at COP 2,000,000 a month and its current term ends on 2027-06-15. My landlord wants to end it at that date simply because he wants to. By what date must he give me written notice, and how much compensation must he pay me?
reference_answer: He must give the written notice, through the authorised postal service, no later than 2027-03-15, three months before the expiry date of 2027-06-15. His full will is a permitted ground only if the contract has run at least four years, and this one will have run almost six. He must compensate the tenant with one and a half months' rent: 1.5 x 2,000,000 = COP 3,000,000 (calculated on the rent in force on the date of the notice, art. 23, point b), paid through the procedure of art. 23, that is deposited in the tenant's favour at the disposal of the competent authority within the three months before the termination date (art. 22, point 8, d), of Ley 820 de 2003).

question: My housing lease in Colombia runs until 2027-12-31 at COP 1,900,000 a month. I want to move out on 2027-04-15 and end the contract. By what date must I send my written notice, how much compensation must I pay, and when must I deposit it?
reference_answer: A tenant may end the contract unilaterally during its initial term or an extension by written notice through the authorised postal service at least three months in advance, and by paying compensation equal to three months' rent (art. 24, point 4, of Ley 820 de 2003). For a leaving date of 2027-04-15 the notice must be sent no later than 2027-01-15. The compensation is 3 x 1,900,000 = COP 5,700,000, calculated on the rent in force on the date of the notice, and it must be deposited in the landlord's favour, at the disposal of the competent authority, in an entity authorised by the national government, within the three months before the leaving date, that is between 2027-01-15 and 2027-04-15 (art. 25, point b).

question: The landlord of my apartment in Colombia failed to do an indispensable repair (not a minor one), and I paid COP 2,000,000 for it myself. Our contract says nothing about deductions and my rent is COP 1,200,000. If I am entitled to recover the cost from the rent, what is the most I can deduct each month and how many months will it take?
reference_answer: Unless the parties agreed otherwise, in the case art. 27 refers to (art. 1993 of the Civil Code, which the corpus does not include) the tenant may deduct the cost of indispensable non-locative repairs from the rent, but never more than 30% of the rent: 30% x 1,200,000 = COP 360,000 a month. Because the total exceeds that amount, the tenant may make periodic deductions of up to 30% of the rent until the whole cost is recovered: 2,000,000 / 360,000 = 5.6, so five deductions of COP 360,000 (1,800,000) and a sixth of COP 200,000, six months in all. If the contract ends before the cost is recovered, the tenant may exercise the right of retention until the landlord has paid the unpaid balance in full (art. 27, last paragraph, and art. 26 of Ley 820 de 2003). Whether the conditions of the Civil Code article are met is not something the corpus can settle.

question: My landlord in Dubai says my security deposit is non-refundable. Is that allowed?
reference_answer: No. When entering into a lease the landlord may obtain a security deposit from the tenant to ensure the property's maintenance at the expiry of the lease, but only on the condition that the landlord undertakes to refund the deposit, or what remains of it, to the tenant when the lease expires (art. 20 of Law No. (26) of 2007). question: Who pays for repairs in an apartment I rent in Dubai, my landlord or me?
reference_answer: Unless the parties agree otherwise, the landlord is responsible, during the term of the lease, for the property's maintenance works and for repairing any defect or damage that may affect the tenant's intended use of it (art. 16 of Law No. (26) of 2007).

question: My landlord in Dubai wants to raise my rent when the lease renews. What notice must he give, and who decides if we cannot agree?
reference_answer: For the purposes of renewing the lease, the landlord and tenant may, before it expires, amend its terms or reconsider increasing or reducing the rent. If they cannot agree, the tribunal may determine the fair rent, taking into account the criteria in art. 9 (art. 13 of Law No. (26) of 2007 as restated by Law No. (33) of 2008). Unless the parties agree otherwise, a party that wants to amend the terms in this way must notify the other at least ninety (90) days before the date on which the lease expires (art. 14).

question: My landlord in Dubai wants me out when my lease ends because he plans to sell the flat. What does he have to do, and can he re-let it afterwards?
reference_answer: When the lease expires, the landlord may seek the tenant's eviction only on the grounds the law lists, which include that the owner wishes to sell the property (art. 25(2)(d) of Law No. (26) of 2007 as restated by Law No. (33) of 2008). He must notify the tenant of the reasons at least twelve (12) months before the date of eviction, and the notice must be served through a Notary Public or by registered mail. The bar on re-letting in art. 26 applies where the tribunal rules for the landlord retaking the property for his own use or his first-degree relatives' use: he may not rent it to a third party for at least two years if it is residential, or the tenant may ask the tribunal for fair compensation. Art. 26 does not mention a sale.

question: When can a landlord in Dubai ask to evict a tenant before the lease ends, and does the tenant keep paying rent while the case is pending?
reference_answer: Before the lease expires the landlord may seek eviction only in the cases the law lists (art. 25(1) of Law No. (26) of 2007 as restated by Law No. (33) of 2008). They include a tenant who does not pay the rent, or any part of it, within thirty (30) days from the date of service of a notice to pay (unless the parties agreed otherwise); one who sublets without the landlord's written approval; one who uses the property for an illegal purpose or for a purpose other than the one it was let for; and one who damages it or endangers its safety. The landlord serves the notice through a Notary Public or by registered mail. Filing a claim to evict does not exempt the tenant from paying the rent for the whole period during which the claim is considered, until an award is rendered and executed (art. 31 of Law No. (26) of 2007).

question: My rent in Dubai is AED 78,000 a year, and the RERA rent index says the average for similar units is AED 100,000. At renewal, what is the most my landlord may raise it?
reference_answer: AED 7,800, so a new rent of AED 85,800. Your rent is 22% below the index average (100,000 - 78,000 = 22,000, which is 22% of 100,000), which falls in the band where the rent is 21% to 30% less than the average rental value of similar units, and for that band the maximum increase on renewal is ten percent (10%) of the rent: 10% of 78,000 is 7,800 (art. 1(d) of Decree No. (43) of 2013 Determining Rent Increases, as reproduced in the Dubai Land Department's Tenancy Guide).

question: In the lease dubai-lease-02, a Jumeirah Village Circle townhouse, clause 7 lets the landlord end the contract at any time on 30 days' notice, and clause 8 ends it automatically if the landlord sells. Are those clauses allowed?
reference_answer: No. A valid lease may not be terminated unilaterally by the landlord or the tenant during its term; it can end only by mutual consent or as the law provides (art. 7 of Law No. (26) of 2007), so a right to end it at any time on 30 days' notice conflicts with the law. And a transfer of ownership does not affect the tenant's right to continue occupying the property under the lease made with the previous owner, provided the lease has a fixed term (art. 28), so a clause ending the contract on a sale also conflicts with it.

question: My landlord in Dubai cut off the water and electricity to my flat after we argued about the rent. Is he allowed to do that, and what can I do?
reference_answer: No. A landlord may not disconnect services from the property or disturb the tenant in his use of the property in any manner. question: My landlord in Dubai phoned me and said I have to leave the flat next month. Does that count as a valid eviction notice?
reference_answer: No. A landlord may seek a tenant's eviction only in the cases listed in art. 25 of Law No. (26) of 2007 as restated by Law No. (33) of 2008, and he must serve a Notice on the tenant through a Notary Public or by registered mail, both for eviction during the lease (paragraph 1) and for eviction when the lease expires (paragraph 2). reference_answer: Where the term of a lease expires but the tenant continues to occupy the property without any objection by the landlord, the lease is renewed for the same term or for a term of one year, whichever is shorter, and under the same terms as the previous lease (art. 6 of Law No. (26) of 2007).

reference_answer: The tenant pays the rent on the dates mutually agreed. Where there is no agreement, or where it is impossible to verify the payment dates, the rent must be paid annually in four equal instalments, in advance (art. 12 of Law No. (26) of 2007).

reference_answer: The term of a lease must be specified. Where it is not specified, or where it is impossible to prove the alleged term, the lease is deemed valid for the period specified for the payment of the rent (art. 5 of Law No. (26) of 2007), so a lease whose rent is paid monthly is deemed valid for a month at a time.

question: I painted my rented flat in Dubai and had built-in wardrobes installed. Was I allowed to, and can I take the wardrobes with me when I leave?
reference_answer: The tenant must maintain the property as an ordinary person would maintain his own. Apart from restorations that were agreed or are customary for tenants, he may not make changes or carry out restoration or maintenance works unless the landlord permits them, and then only after obtaining the required licences from the competent official entities (art. 19 of Law No. (26) of 2007). Unless the parties agree otherwise, when vacating and surrendering possession the tenant may not remove the leasehold improvements he made (art. 23), so the wardrobes stay.

question: My landlord in Dubai wants me out when my lease expires so that his daughter can live in the flat. What must he show, how much notice must he give, and can he rent it to someone else afterwards?
reference_answer: On expiry of the lease the owner may seek eviction to retake possession for his own use or for use by any of his first-degree relatives, a daughter being one, only if he proves that he does not own any alternative property that is suitable for that purpose (art. 25, paragraph 2(c), of Law No. (26) of 2007 as restated by Law No. (33) of 2008). He must notify the tenant of the reasons at least twelve months before the date of eviction, by a notice served through a Notary Public or by registered mail (art. 25, paragraph 2). If the Tribunal rules for the landlord on that ground, he may not rent the property to a third party before at least two years have passed from the date he retook possession, for residential property, or three years for non-residential property; otherwise the tenant may ask the Tribunal to award him fair compensation (art. 26).

question: My landlord in Dubai says he will demolish the building and rebuild it. What must he do before I can be evicted, and will I be able to come back, and at what rent?
reference_answer: On expiry of the lease the landlord may seek eviction because the owner wishes to demolish and reconstruct the property, or to add new structures that would prevent the tenant from using it, only if he obtains the required permits from the competent entities (art. 25, paragraph 2(a), of Law No. (26) of 2007 as restated by Law No. (33) of 2008). He must notify the tenant of the reasons at least twelve months before the date of eviction, by a notice served through a Notary Public or by registered mail (art. 25, paragraph 2). Where the property is demolished and reconstructed, or renovated and restored, by the landlord, the tenant has a right of first refusal to return to it, and the rent is determined in accordance with art. 9 (art. 29, paragraph 1): the rent the parties specify, or failing that the rental value of similar property, which the Tribunal determines. The tenant must exercise the right within 30 days of being notified of it by the landlord (art. 29, paragraph 2).

question: I sublet a room in my rented flat in Dubai. What happens to the subtenant and to me if my landlord did not agree, and what if he did agree and my own lease later ends?
reference_answer: Unless the parties agree otherwise, the tenant may not assign the use of the property or sub-let it to third parties unless the landlord has given written consent (art. 24 of Law No. (26) of 2007). If he sub-lets without the landlord's written approval, the landlord may seek eviction of the tenant and of the subtenant, and the subtenant keeps the right to claim compensation from the tenant (art. 25, paragraph 1(b), as restated by Law No. (33) of 2008). A sub-lease ends when the lease between the landlord and the tenant ends, unless the landlord expressly agrees to extend it (art. 8). If the Tribunal ends the lease and the property is occupied by a subtenant under a contract made with the tenant and approved by the landlord, the subtenant may continue to occupy it on the terms of the sub-lease (art. 30).

question: How do Spain, Colombia and Dubai treat a security deposit in a housing lease?
reference_answer: Spain: the landlord must require a cash deposit (fianza) of one month's rent for a dwelling, and the parties may agree an additional guarantee of up to two months' rent in leases of up to five years, or seven if the landlord is a legal person (art. 36 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos). Colombia: in housing leases no cash deposits or other real guarantees may be demanded to secure the tenant's obligations under the contract (art. 16 of Ley 820 de 2003). Dubai: the landlord may take a security deposit to ensure the property's maintenance at the end of the lease, only on the undertaking to refund it, or what remains of it, when the lease expires; the indexed text sets no amount (art. 20 of Law No. (26) of 2007).

question: If the owner of a rented home sells it, does the tenant have to leave? Compare Spain and Dubai.
reference_answer: Spain: the buyer of a rented dwelling is subrogated in the landlord's rights and obligations for the first five years of the contract, or seven if the previous landlord was a legal person, even if he meets the requirements of art. 34 of the Mortgage Law. If the agreed duration is longer, the buyer is subrogated for all of it unless he meets those requirements, in which case he must bear the lease only for the time left of the five (seven) years and the seller must compensate the tenant with one month's rent for each remaining year beyond that. If the parties stipulated that a sale ends the lease, the buyer need bear it only for the time left of the five (seven) years (art. 14 of the Ley de Arrendamientos Urbanos).
